title: Directives
body:
Lines that tell the **assembler** something rather than telling the [[CPU]] something. They
generate no opcode; they reserve space, define constants, or control how the source is
translated. Also called pseudo-ops, because they sit in the instruction column but are not
[[Instructions]].

## Defining data

| Directive | Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `dc.b` / `dc.w` / `dc.l` | **define constant**: emit these bytes here | `msg: dc.b 'Hello',0` |
| `ds.b` / `ds.w` / `ds.l` | **define storage**: reserve $n$ units, uninitialised | `buf: ds.b 80` |
| `equ` | name a value, no space used | `SIZE: equ 80` |

`dc` puts bytes in the object file; `ds` only reserves room. `equ` is neither, it is a
compile-time substitution, the assembly equivalent of `#define`.

The label on such a line becomes the [[Addressing Modes|absolute address]] of the data, which
is what makes `move.l #msg,a0` (address of) different from `move.l msg,d0` (contents of).

## Controlling the assembly

| Directive | Means |
|---|---|
| `org` | assemble the following code starting at this address |
| `even` / `align` | pad so the next item starts at an even address |
| `end` | end of source; anything after it is ignored |
| `xdef` / `xref` | export a label, import one defined elsewhere |
| `section` | which segment this goes in (text, data, bss) |

`even` is the one that bites. The 68000 raises an **address error** on any word or longword
access at an odd address, so an odd-length `dc.b` string followed by a `dc.w` puts the word
at an odd address and the program dies three bombs in. Put `even` after every byte-sized data
block and the problem never happens. See [[Assembly Errors]].

`xdef` and `xref` are the other half of link-time errors: `xref` promises a label exists
somewhere, and the linker is the one that finds out it does not.
